summary:
Tyumen Oblast stands under the Russian national framework as it operates across all the country's regions. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records no region-specific findings: it sets the national conditions in force here and everywhere else in Russia.

Same-sex activity is not criminalised. Same-sex marriage and legal gender transition are banned, trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, and no discrimination legislation based on sexual orientation or gender identity covers housing, healthcare or employment.

'Gay propaganda' offences carry fines up to 400,000 roubles (about £3,600) for individuals or up to 15 days' detention, and repeat offences can bring criminal prosecution with up to four years in prison. The November 2023 Supreme Court 'extremist' designation of the international LGBT+ movement makes participation punishable by two to six years and organising by six to ten years.

Enforcement volume is documented. Between December 2022 and March 2024 at least 139 people were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions tied to the 'International Public LGBT Movement' designation, approximately 98 administrative and three criminal.

The designation entered into force in January 2024 and, in Human Rights Watch's assessment, opened the way to arbitrary prosecutions of LGBT people and their supporters. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation; two were sentenced to prison and one died by suicide in pretrial detention.

Displaying banned symbols is itself a chargeable act. Human Rights Watch counted 81 people found guilty of administrative offences across 98 court cases for displaying banned symbols, with fines up to 2,000 roubles; a repeat display is punishable under the criminal code by up to four years in prison.

On 15 May 2025 investigators charged three publishing-house staff under article 282.2 for selling fiction exploring LGBT themes, a charge carrying up to 12 years.

The Home Office note assesses that trans people, publicly active LGBT+ advocates and people in the North Caucasus are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. A transgender visitor entering Tyumen Oblast is therefore exposed to a national regime under which expression, association and document-based identity are all policed, and under which the visitor's status as transgender is itself grounds for the treatment the assessing authority classifies as persecution.
tangentialFactors:
The formal decriminalisation of same-sex activity coexists with heavy penalties for expression and association, so an arrest record here is more likely to arise from what a person says, displays or joins than from private conduct.

The enforcement mix is overwhelmingly administrative: of the 101 extremism-related convictions Human Rights Watch recorded, roughly 98 were administrative and three criminal, and the largest single block, 81 people across 98 court cases, concerned display of banned symbols. Criminal exposure sits on top of that layer rather than replacing it, with at least 20 criminal charges brought between January 2024 and June 2025.

The escalation is visible in both breadth and severity. Symbol display draws fines measured in thousands of roubles on a first instance, while the same conduct a second time, participation in a designated organisation, or leadership of one moves into multi-year prison terms, and the publishing-house charges under article 282.2 reach 12 years.

A death in pretrial detention was recorded among those held on designation-related charges, and Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to people fleeing Russia. The Home Office standard of persecution for trans people shapes how that flight is assessed elsewhere.

The US State Department advises Level 4, Do Not Travel for Russia, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers, and the official Russian national warning to LGBT travellers confirms the same risk from the other side.
localsOnly:
Residents of Tyumen Oblast have no statutory protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in housing, healthcare or employment; no such legislation covers these fields.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023. Document markers cannot be changed and trans-specific healthcare was effectively prohibited, so a resident's identity papers will continue to carry a sex marker that conflicts with their presentation.

Same-sex marriage is banned, and no partner recognition regime exists for same-sex couples.

Participation in the 'international LGBT movement' designated by the Supreme Court in November 2023 is punishable by two to six years, and organising by six to ten years. Displaying banned symbols is treated as an administrative offence on a first instance, with a fine up to 2,000 roubles, and as a criminal offence on repetition, carrying up to four years.

'Gay propaganda' offences expose residents to fines up to 400,000 roubles or up to 15 days' detention, with repeat offences prosecutable for up to four years.

At least 139 people were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws between December 2022 and March 2024, and Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions by 30 June 2025. Staff of a publishing house were charged on 15 May 2025 under article 282.2 for selling fiction exploring LGBT themes, facing up to 12 years.

Coercive conversion practice is documented: BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman was held for nine months from summer 2021 in a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour, before escaping after police responded to a phone she had found.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no Tyumen Oblast-specific enforcement data. Neither the Home Office note nor the Human Rights Watch report breaks its figures down by federal subject, so how many of the 139 people affected, the 101 convictions or the 98 symbol-display cases fell in this oblast is not sourced here.

Local policing practice in Tyumen Oblast, the availability of friendly legal representation, and the treatment of transgender detainees in the oblast's pretrial facilities are not sourced in this inventory.

The conditions under which a transgender visitor would be identified at border control or during any administrative stop, including whether document sex markers are checked against presentation, are not stated in the sources reviewed.

Human Rights Watch's figure of approximately 98 administrative and three criminal convictions is the report's own approximation and is reproduced as reported; the underlying case records are not itemised in this inventory.

Whether article 282.2 as applied to the publishing-house staff would be charged against a foreign visitor for purchasing or carrying the same material is not addressed by any source listed here.

The Home Office note's persecution assessment governs UK asylum claims; equivalent standards in other receiving states are outside this inventory.
